passages.t: Hezekiah's scribes, and humility at court
passages.happening:
A new heading opens the next collection: ‘These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah’ (verse 1).

‘It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out’ (verse 2). ‘As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched’ (verse 3). Remove the dross from silver and a silversmith can make something fine; remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness (verses 4-5).

Do not push yourself forward before the king or take your place among the great. It is better to be invited up higher than to be sent down in front of everyone (verses 6-7). Do not rush into court against your neighbor, or betray another person's secret in the dispute, or you will be shamed (verses 8-10).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 25 to 29 are the book's second collection of Solomon's proverbs. The heading shows wisdom being handed on: first spoken, then gathered by later scribes who judged it worth keeping for their own day.

Hezekiah reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC. He is remembered as a king who trusted the LORD, restored worship at the temple, and survived the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC. Many scholars think his reign saw a revival of writing in Jerusalem, especially after refugees came south when Samaria fell in 722 BC. The heading does not say how these sayings had been kept until then, in writing or by word of mouth.

Glory, kavod, comes from a word meaning heavy or weighty. Verse 2 sets God's glory in what he hides and a king's glory in searching it out. Even a king's understanding works within limits God has set.

At a royal gathering, guests stood or sat by rank, and taking a higher place than one's due risked public shame when the host moved you down.
passages.later: Jesus gave the same advice about the place of honor at a wedding feast: “But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place” (Luke 14:10), so that the host will invite you to move up, and ‘Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you’ (Luke 14:10). And Moses said of what God hides: ‘The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us’ (Deuteronomy 29:29).
passages.asks: It is better to be invited up than sent down. Ask where you are pushing for a place of honor that is not yours to take. And ask whether there is a dispute you are rushing into that a quiet conversation could settle.

passages.t: Apples of gold, and songs to a heavy heart
passages.happening:
This part is a string of pictures. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (verse 11). ‘Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man’s rebuke to a listening ear’ (verse 12). A trustworthy messenger is like ‘the cold of snow in the time of harvest’ (verse 13). ‘Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given’ (verse 14). ‘Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone’ (verse 15).

‘If you find honey, eat just what you need’ (verse 16). ‘Seldom set foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he grow weary and hate you’ (verse 17). A false witness is ‘Like a club or sword or sharp arrow’ (verse 18). Trusting a faithless man in trouble is like leaning on ‘a broken tooth or a foot out of joint’ (verse 19).

And ‘Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
This collection loves the comparison proverb, two things set side by side, often with no verb. The reader has to work out the link. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in silver settings because both are beautiful and fitting.

Snow at harvest most likely means snow brought down from the mountains to cool drinks in the heat of the grain harvest, a luxury. Rain at harvest would be unwelcome, but cold refreshment was a gift. A trustworthy messenger is that kind of relief.

Clouds and wind without rain disappoint a farmer waiting for water. So does a man who boasts of gifts he never gives.

Verse 20 is a gentle warning. Cheerful songs do not help a heavy heart. They can sting like vinegar on a wound. Sometimes the kindest thing is to sit quietly with someone who grieves.
passages.later: Paul gives the counsel verse 20 implies: ‘Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep’ (Romans 12:15).
passages.asks: A word at the right moment is like gold in silver. Ask who needs a fitting word from you this week, and who needs your quiet company more than your cheerfulness. And ask whether you have promised anything, like rainless clouds, that you have not given.

passages.t: Feed your enemy, and a city without walls
passages.happening:
“If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you” (verses 21-22).

‘As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks’ (verse 23). ‘Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife’ (verse 24). ‘Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land’ (verse 25). A righteous man who gives way before the wicked is ‘Like a muddied spring or a polluted well’ (verse 26).

‘It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory’ (verse 27). And ‘Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Verses 21 and 22 ask for kindness to an enemy, not just restraint. Burning coal is gechel. Most interpreters take the coals as the burning shame or remorse that kindness can stir, which may lead the enemy to change. Others suggest a background in an ancient ritual of repentance. Either way, the kindness is real food and real water.

The north wind that brings rain is puzzling, since rain in Israel usually comes from the west. Interpreters suggest a local wind, a northwestern wind, or a saying borrowed from another region.

Verse 24 repeats 21:9. Living on a corner of a flat roof would be cramped and exposed. It is a picture of a home without peace, not a comment on women in general, and the book warns just as plainly about angry men.

The chapter is framed by searching and glory: it is a king's glory to search out a matter (verse 2), and it is not good to search out one's own glory (verse 27). A city with broken walls had no defense. Neither does a person who cannot rule his temper.
passages.later: Paul quotes verses 21 and 22 and adds his own conclusion: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). The law already asked for help to an enemy: ‘If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him’ (Exodus 23:4).
passages.asks: Kindness to an enemy is the chapter's hardest command. Ask who you think of as an enemy, and what one practical kindness to them would look like. And ask where your own walls are broken down, the places where your temper has no guard.
